en: The supplement consists of eulogies of Bāṇa:
some on the subject of punning, some on the art of word-composition, and others on aesthetic flavor (rasa).
Whether it be in the description of ornaments, in the depiction of certain noble subjects, or in other poetic narratives—alas!
Everywhere, Bāṇa is like a five-headed lion who shatters the temples of the elephant-like poets, roaming with mastery through the Vindhya forest of profound, steady, and peerless poetry. (1)
Where are those hundreds of loads of gold or those herds of rutting elephants offered today by Śrī Harṣa to the poet Bāṇa from [the treasury] of Śrī Candradeva?
I believe that those glories of his, which were engraved by Bāṇa with clusters of eloquent verses, do not undergo even the slightest fading even at the dissolution of the eon.
(In the *Vyaktiviveka-vyākhyāna* composed by Ruyyaka:
"Alas, I worship Abhinanda, the lord of meaning; I praise Vākpatirāja, the lord of speech;
I bow to Kālidāsa, the lord of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*); and I am prostrate before Bāṇa, the lord of all. (3)

In this [work], the Goddess of Speech has been cultivated with aesthetic flavor by many kings of poets; however, because of his unique nature, Bāṇa calls her simply "Vāṇī" (The Arrow). (From the *Udayasundarī* by Soḍḍhala)
Like the ocean, Bāṇa attained fame through the narrative called *Harṣacarita* in the heart of the wise— the brother of Kādambarī and the very nectar of Viśveśvara.
By means of his bow alone— which was ever accompanied by arrows, assumed a downward-curved form,
and was rich in strings— he completely won over all people.
(Regarding Trivikrama:
Just as Śikhaṇḍinī was previously born as Śikhaṇḍin, I understand that Vāṇī became Bāṇa in order to attain greater boldness. // 7 //
Even if the pace of the verses is slow, the reason for it is the arrow lodged in the heart of Govardhana, which causes the restlessness of the deer-like poets. (8)
Subandhu, Bāṇabhaṭṭa, and Kavirāja—these three are experts in the path of *vakrokti* (circuitous expression); whether a fourth exists or not remains to be seen. (9)
Like King Śrī Harṣa, the lord of the earth brought about a union between Bāṇa and Mayūra, who were captivating through their variegated and elegant compositions.

Victorious is the illustrious Bhaṭṭabāṇa, the king of poets, who is an arrow that pierces the armor of rival poets, a peacock roaming through the dense forest of the trees of poetic composition, and a close friend to the world of connoisseurs. (From the *Navasāhasāṅka*) 11.
(Vīranārāyaṇacarita) It is fitting that poets have adopted silence upon hearing the Kādambarī,
for there is a traditional rule that an interruption of study occurs at the sound of an arrow.
With its beautiful sounds, colors, and words, and possessing aesthetic flavor and emotion, it captivates the minds of the world;
yet is this not a young woman?
No, no—it is the speech of Bāṇa, whose nature is sweet. (13)
Accompanied by the deeds of Harṣa and constantly featuring the story of Kādambarī,
Bāṇa’s prose wanders freely upon the earth like a woman who has not yet been married.
What poet can ever equal Bāṇa, who is like the speech of a great sage?
What jewel can ever follow the ocean, or what gem can rival the sun? (15)
In the *Raghunāthacarita*, it is held that the *pāñcālī* style (*rīti*) consists of an equal arrangement of word and meaning;
this [style] is found in the speech of Śilābhaṭṭārikā and in the compositions of Bāṇa. (16)
Even a single arrow, when flashing forth, renders poets devoid of pride; how much more so when it is accompanied by Pulinda, who has prepared his aim?
When the name "Daṇḍin" is uttered, the minds of poets tremble immediately;
but once Bāṇa has entered within, it is speech itself that is obstructed at the throat. (Of Dhanapāla). 18.
